summary: : Mr. Sanjay Sen, Sr. Adv. Mr. Adarsh Tripathi Mr. Vikram Singh Baid Mr. Ajitesh Garg 8. During the proceedings before the Central Commission, Record of Proceedings dated 24.05.2016 was issued seeking certain information, clarifications and details from the Appellant in relation to the tariff petition. According to the Appellant, no specific information or justification was sought by the Central Commission in respect of the Wagon Tippler and associated works claimed under additional capitalization. 9. On 14.07.2016, the Appellant furnished the information and clarifications sought by the Central Commission pursuant to the Record of Proceedings dated 24.05.2016. 11. Aggrieved by the aforesaid disallowance, the Appellant filed Review Petition No. 14 of 2017 before the Central Commission seeking review of the Order dated 16.02.2017. 12. The Central Commission, however, dismissed the Review Petition No. 14 of 2017 vide Order dated 31.08.2017 (Review Order). 13. Aggrieved by the Impugned Order, the Appellant has filed the present Appeal before us challenging the disallowance of additional capitalization towards Wagon Tippler and associated works. _“(i) Allow the appeal and set aside the order dated 16.02.2017 passed by the Central Commission to the extent challenged in the present appeal; and_ _(ii) Pass such other Order(s) and this Hon’ble Tribunal may deem just and proper.”_ that the disallowance is inconsistent with the settled regulatory and judicial position subsequently recognized by this Tribunal. 18. It was pointed out that the Commission, by order dated 27.04.2023 in Petition No. 441/GT/2020, made the said claim subject to the final outcome of the present Appeal. The Wagon Tippler works were ultimately capitalized in FY 201920 and were accordingly claimed in the truing up petition for the tariff period 201924 along with detailed justifications and supporting documents. 31. On the aforesaid grounds, the Appellant prayed that the disallowance of additional capitalization towards Wagon Tippler and associated works be set aside and the claim be allowed. 40. It was also pointed out that despite the said letter being of the year 2004, NTPC never raised any claim for Wagon Tipplers during the tariff periods 200409 and 2009-14. Reliance is placed upon the judgment of this Tribunal dated 10.02.2015 in _**Power Grid Corporation of India Limited vs. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors., Appeal No. 13 of 2014**_ , wherein it was held that assertions made in affidavits cannot be accepted in tariff proceedings in the absence of documentary or supporting evidence. 51. In the Impugned Order, the CERC had rejected the claim with following observations on the above justification: _(i) Liabilities to meet award of arbitration or for compliance of the order or decree of a court of law;_ _(v) Any liability for works executed prior to the cut-off date, after prudence check of the details of such undischarged liability, total estimated cost of package, reasons for such withholding of payment and release of such payments etc.;_ direct the NTPC to furnish the same. Admittedly, no such direction to seek clarification or additional information was issued by the CERC on the issue of additional capitalization for wagon tippler and associated works; though a direction was issued as part of Record of Proceeding date 24.05.2016 in respect of certain other issues relevant to tariff determination. In this background, we are of the opinion that the claim of the Appellant-Petitioner NTPC could not have been rejected on the ground of non-submission of documentary evidence. 56. In the Review Order, CERC has relied on the Section 101 of the Evidence Act to fault NTPC for non-submission of the documentary evidence. This contention has also been advanced by GRIDCO in its submissions. 58. In view of the statutory framework and the settled principles governing quasi-judicial proceedings, it follows that proceedings before the Commission are not strictly bound by the technical rules of evidence embodied in the Indian Evidence Act, unless such requirement is expressly incorporated by the governing statute. 61. However, in our opinion, the Appellant-Petitioner had not furnished a clearly articulated justification in support of its claim. A party to any proceeding ought not to remain complacent regarding the outcome and must place on record a proper and cogent rationale for the relief sought. Such rationale should, as far as possible, anticipate potential objections from the opposing parties as well as issues that may reasonably arise in the mind of the adjudicatory forum. 67. We have perused this Tribunal’s judgement in _**Power Grid Corporation of India Limited vs. Central Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors., Appeal No. 13 of 2014,**_ which has been relied upon by GRIDCO to support its contention that in the tariff proceedings, mere assertions or averments unsupported by documentary evidence cannot be accepted by the Commission. We find that the facts of the present case are different from that in Appeal No. 13 of 2014. In _**PGCIL vs. CERC & Ors., Appeal No. 13 of 2014**_ , the Commission had, in the first instance, directed PGCIL to file affidavit explaining the delay. It was only after examining the contents of the affidavit that CERC had allowed part of the expenditure, while disallowing the remaining in the absence of proper justification backed by documentary evidence. In the case in hand, CERC had not directed NTPC to file affidavit on the aspect of additional capitalisation for wagon tippler and associated work. affected beneficiaries shall also be given opportunity to respond to the justification and documents submitted by NTPC in support of its claim. The matter is remanded to the Central Commission for fresh consideration of the Appellant’s claim in accordance with law and after affording opportunity of hearing to all concerned parties. The Captioned Appeal and pending IAs, if any, are disposed of in the above terms.
